name: Blue Pill STM32F103C8T6
flash: 64KB (the chip on most boards actually has 128KB, but don’t count on it; plan for 64KB)

buses.i2c: I2C1: SCL PB6 / SDA PB7 (default); SCL PB8 / SDA PB9 (remapped; this course uses this pair for the OLED, with Wire.setSDA(PB9); Wire.setSCL(PB8); in code); I2C2: SCL PB10 / SDA PB11
buses.spi: SPI1: SCK PA5 / MISO PA6 / MOSI PA7 / NSS PA4; SPI2: SCK PB13 / MISO PB14 / MOSI PB15 / NSS PB12
buses.uart: UART1: TX PA9 / RX PA10 (Serial uses this pair by default; you need a USB-TTL adapter); UART2: TX PA2 / RX PA3; UART3: TX PB10 / RX PB11

power: 3.3V logic. 5V-tolerant (FT) pins: PA8-PA15, PB2-PB15, PC13-PC15. NOT 5V-tolerant: PA0-PA7, PB0, PB1 (anything with an ADC function). The 5V header pin is straight from USB; 3.3V comes from a small onboard LDO with only about 100-150mA to spare for peripherals: fine for an OLED and sensors, not for servos or LED strips
flash_how: The board has no built-in programmer, so buy an ST-Link V2 (the USB-stick style one, about $8-12). Use 4 jumper wires to connect the ST-Link’s 3.3V, SWDIO, SWCLK and GND to the 4 header pins at the bottom of the board (labeled 3.3 / SWIO / SWCLK / GND), plug the ST-Link into your computer’s USB port, then run pio run -t upload. Leave both yellow jumpers (BOOT0/BOOT1) in their default 0 position; flashing over ST-Link doesn’t require touching them. The board’s micro-USB port only supplies power by default; it can’t flash and isn’t a serial port (unless you set up USB CDC separately). For serial output, buy a separate USB-TTL adapter and connect it to PA9/PA10
gotchas: The onboard LED on PC13 is active-low: digitalWrite(PC13, LOW) turns it on, the opposite of the UNO
PC13 has very weak drive (about 3mA); it can only light its own LED. Don’t use it to drive anything else

Many cheap boards carry a CKS32/GD32 compatible chip rather than a genuine ST part. If ST-Link reports UNEXPECTED idcode or unknown device, that’s usually why; add upload_flags = -c set CPUTAPID 0x2ba01477 to platformio.ini

Serial goes out the PA9/PA10 hardware UART by default, not USB. Plugging the board’s USB port into your computer won’t create a serial device; you need a separate USB-TTL adapter (TX to RX, RX to TX, crossed over!)

To use the USB port as a serial port, add build_flags = -D PIO_FRAMEWORK_ARDUINO_ENABLE_CDC -D USBCON to platformio.ini. Also, many boards ship with the wrong USB D+ pull-up resistor (R10, 10kΩ instead of 1.5kΩ), so the computer won’t recognize the board until you swap it for 1.5kΩ
PA0-PA7, PB0 and PB1 are not 5V-tolerant. Don’t connect a 5V sensor’s output directly to these pins; use FT pins like PB10-PB15, or add a voltage divider
PB3, PB4 and PA15 are taken by JTAG by default. STM32duino releases them automatically when you call pinMode, but if one of these pins acts strangely, suspect this first
PA11 and PA12 are USB D-/D+ and have pull-up resistors on the board; avoid using them as ordinary GPIO
Power the board only through USB 5V or the 3.3 header pin. Don’t feed the 5V header pin from a 3.3V supply, and don’t power it from two places at once
Flash is nominally 64KB; U8g2 plus a CJK font can easily blow past it. Watch the Flash usage percentage when you compile

left.name: VBAT
left.note: RTC backup battery; you won't need it for now

left.name: PC13
left.note: The onboard LED is on this pin. Active-low (lights when LOW). Weak drive; don't hang a big load on it

left.name: PC14
left.note: For the external 32.768kHz crystal; normally not used as GPIO

left.name: PA0
left.note: Task 3-1 reads the potentiometer on this pin

left.name: R
left.note: Pull to ground to reset, same as pressing the RESET button
Chip supply. Power your sensors from here too

left.name: GND
left.note: Every ground must be tied together. Forgetting a common ground is the second most common beginner mistake

right.name: 5V
right.note: 5V straight from USB. Power 5V modules from here

right.name: PB9
right.note: SDA for the OLED in Task 3-3

right.name: PB8
right.note: SCL for the OLED in Task 3-3

right.name: PB4
right.note: Taken by JTAG by default; release it before using it as GPIO

right.name: PA12
right.note: USB data line. Leave it alone when using USB serial

right.name: PA10
right.note: Task 2-1: connect to the serial adapter's TX

right.name: PA9
right.note: Task 2-1: connect to the serial adapter's RX. TX goes to RX, crossed over!
